global_lexicon.core_thesis: Wastewater membrane bioreactors (MBRs) suffer from unpredictable membrane fouling and high energy consumption, which can be mitigated by an integrated three-layer paradigm coupling machine learning for accurate prediction, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) for auditable interpretability, and digital twins (DT) for real-time operational simulation and decision support.

key_terms.definition: An advanced wastewater treatment process combining biological activated sludge treatment with low-pressure membrane separation (microfiltration or ultrafiltration).
The pressure gradient across the membrane that drives permeate flux, serving as the primary operational indicator of membrane fouling progression.
High-molecular-weight microbial biopolymers composed of polysaccharides, proteins, and humic substances that form the cake layer and drive biofouling.
Soluble microbial excretion products that penetrate membrane pores, causing irreversible pore narrowing and adsorptive fouling.
A hydraulic filtration model that partitions total membrane resistance into intrinsic membrane resistance, reversible cake resistance, and irreversible pore blocking resistance.
The permeate flux threshold below which fouling occurs slowly and reversibly, and above which rapid irreversible fouling accumulation takes place.
Analytical techniques such as SHAP and LIME that decompose black-box ML model outputs into human-interpretable feature attributions to provide operational transparency and regulatory trust.
A game-theoretic framework based on Shapley values that computes additive feature attribution values explaining individual model predictions.
An explanation technique that builds an interpretable surrogate model around a specific prediction instance by perturbing inputs.
A continuously updated virtual replica of a physical MBR facility bidirectionally coupled via real-time SCADA sensor streams, combining mechanistic models (ASM) and ML predictions.
A three-tier taxonomy consisting of Tier I (Descriptive monitoring and asset status), Tier II (Predictive forecasting and fault detection), and Tier III (Prescriptive closed-loop autonomous control).
Mechanistic biokinetic model family (ASM1, ASM2d, ASM3) simulating biological nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic removal in wastewater treatment.

global_context_pack:
Core Thesis: Wastewater membrane bioreactors (MBRs) suffer from unpredictable membrane fouling and elevated aeration energy consumption, which can be overcome by an integrated three-tier paradigm combining machine learning (the predictive engine), explainable artificial intelligence (the interpretability and regulatory trust layer), and digital twins (the closed-loop operational integration layer).

Output Language: English

Glossary of Acronyms and Terms:
- MBR: Membrane Bioreactor
- TMP: Transmembrane Pressure
- ML: Machine Learning
- XAI: Explainable Artificial Intelligence
- DT: Digital Twin
- EPS: Extracellular Polymeric Substances
- SMP: Soluble Microbial Products
- MLSS: Mixed Liquor Suspended Solids
- SRT: Solids Retention Time
- HRT: Hydraulic Retention Time
- DO: Dissolved Oxygen
- SHAP: SHapley Additive exPlanations
- LIME: Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations
- PDP: Partial Dependence Plot
- BSM-MBR: Benchmark Simulation Model for Membrane Bioreactors
- ASM: Activated Sludge Model
- SEC: Specific Energy Consumption

Document Outline & Structure:
- Abstract: Scope, core findings, predictive ML models, XAI methods, digital twin frameworks, and implementation barriers in MBRs.
- Section 1: Introduction: MBR operational advantages, fouling and energy liabilities, black-box limitations of ML, integrated ML-XAI-DT framework, and review objectives.
- Section 2: Methodology: Literature search protocol across Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed (2010–2025) and study selection criteria.
- Section 3: Machine Learning for Membrane Fouling Prediction: Fouling mechanisms and resistance-in-series modeling (3.1); shallow and kernel-based models such as SVM and LSSVM (3.2); ensemble methods and deep architectures like RF and LSTM (3.3); dataset limitations, overfitting, and cross-site generalizability (3.4).
- Section 4: Explainable Artificial Intelligence in MBR Applications: Regulatory imperative in water systems (4.1); SHAP framework and dominant operational predictors including MLSS, SRT, HRT, and aeration intensity (4.2); LIME, PDP, and gradient-based attribution methods (4.3).
- Section 5: ML-Driven Energy Optimization in MBR Systems: Energy structure and aeration targets (5.1); confirmed energy reduction evidence (up to 20% aeration savings) and operational research gaps (5.2).
- Section 6: Digital Twin Frameworks for MBR Systems: Architecture, components, and three maturity tiers (Descriptive, Predictive, Prescriptive) (6.1); XAI integration into DT decision architectures (6.2).
- Section 7: Research Gaps and Future Directions: Nine critical research gaps covering benchmark datasets, uncertainty quantification, full-scale DT evidence, dynamic influent monitoring, regulatory acceptance, economic costs, human workforce requirements, non-ML baseline comparisons, and computational footprints.
- Section 8: Conclusions: Key takeaways across fouling prediction, XAI-driven transparency, digital twin frontiers, and multi-disciplinary pathways toward trustworthy autonomous MBR management.
